title: Driving Hungover: Is It Safe or Legal the Morning After?
excerpt: Can you drive hungover? Why you can still be over the limit the morning after, how a hangover affects driving even at zero BAC, morning-after DUI risk, and why no formula tells you when it is safe.
metaDescription: Can you drive hungover? Why you may still be over the limit the next morning, how hangovers slow driving even at zero BAC, and morning-after DUI risk.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** you can legally drive hungover as long as your blood alcohol is under the limit, but that's a lower bar than "safe to drive." Two things work against you the morning after a big night. First, there may still be alcohol in your blood, sometimes enough to be over the legal limit, even though you've slept. Second, even once the alcohol is gone, a hangover itself slows your reactions and attention in ways research has compared to mild intoxication. If you drank heavily, the safest move is to wait, get a ride, or take transit.

**The quick rules:** Nothing speeds up how fast your body clears alcohol, and no formula can tell you the moment you're safe to drive. If you drank heavily last night, plan the morning without driving: arrange a ride, take transit, or let someone else drive. If you feel foggy, shaky, nauseous, or sleepy, don't drive, even if you think the alcohol has cleared. And remember that legal limits are lower for commercial drivers, drivers under 21, and in some places.

> **When to get help, not just a ride.** Most hangovers are miserable but harmless. Get medical care right away (call 911 in the US) if someone who drank is confused, hard to wake, vomiting repeatedly, having seizures, breathing slowly or irregularly, or has pale or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a hangover, and they need emergency care. If you wake up with shaking hands, sweating, a racing heart, or anxiety that eases when you drink again, that can be alcohol withdrawal rather than an ordinary hangover. It's worth telling a doctor about, plainly and without embarrassment. Either way, nobody in that state should be driving.

## Can You Drive Hungover? The Two Separate Problems

When people ask whether they can drive hungover, they're usually blending two different questions:

1. **Is there still alcohol in my blood?** This is the legal question. It's about your blood alcohol concentration (BAC), the share of your blood that is alcohol. If it's over the limit, you can be arrested for a DUI no matter how you feel.
2. **Am I actually fit to drive?** This is the safety question. It's about your reaction time, attention, judgment, and alertness. A hangover can hurt all of those even at a BAC of zero.

Most people only think about the first question, and they usually answer it with a guess based on how they feel. That's the trap. Feeling "mostly okay" is a poor guide to your BAC, and passing the legal test doesn't mean your brain is back to full speed.

## Can You Still Be Over the Limit the Next Morning?

Yes, and this catches a lot of people off guard.

Your liver breaks down alcohol at a fairly steady pace. A common rule of thumb is that the body clears about one standard drink per hour, which works out to BAC dropping by somewhere around 0.015% per hour for many adults. The exact rate varies with body size, sex, genetics, liver health, and how much you drink regularly, but the key point holds: **the clock only starts running from your peak, and nothing you do in the morning makes it run faster.** (Our guide to [what BAC means](/never-hungover/what-is-bac) explains how it's measured and what affects it.)

Here's what that looks like in practice. Say you had eight or nine drinks over an evening and finished at 1 a.m. Your BAC may have peaked well above 0.08%. Even if you slept six or seven hours, there's a real chance you still had measurable alcohol in your blood when you woke up, and depending on how high you peaked, you could still be near or over the limit at breakfast.

A few things make morning-after alcohol more likely:

- **Drinking late.** The later your last drink, the less time your body has had before you need to drive.
- **A long, heavy night.** Ten drinks take roughly twice as long to clear as five.
- **Shots and strong cocktails.** These deliver more alcohol than people tend to count. A large pour of wine or a double counts as more than one drink.
- **Smaller body size.** The same number of drinks produces a higher BAC in a smaller person.
- **Sleep doesn't help.** Sleep passes time, but it doesn't speed up how fast your liver works. You wake up with exactly as much alcohol as the hours allowed you to clear.

Our article on [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system) walks through these timelines in more detail.

### Why "I slept it off" is not a plan

There's a common belief that a night's sleep resets you. It doesn't. Sleep after drinking is also usually poor quality: alcohol helps you fall asleep but tends to break up sleep in the second half of the night, so you often wake up tired as well as hungover. That leaves you with leftover alcohol, a hangover, and a sleep debt all at once. Each of those hurts driving on its own.

## Is Driving Hungover as Dangerous as Driving Drunk?

Not identical, but closer than most people assume, even when there's no alcohol left at all.

The best-known research here comes from a group at Utrecht University in the Netherlands led by Joris Verster. In a 2014 driving-simulator study, healthy young adults drove a long, monotonous highway route twice: once on a normal morning and once the morning after a night of drinking, after their BAC had returned to zero. When hungover, they weaved within their lane more (researchers measure this as "standard deviation of lateral position," which is just how much the car drifts side to side) and their driving was less steady overall. The researchers compared the size of the change to what they'd expect from someone driving with a BAC of around 0.05%.

That study has limits. It was done in a simulator, with a fairly small group of young volunteers, after a specific amount of drinking. It doesn't tell you exactly how impaired *you* will be. But it fits with a broader body of research showing that hangovers slow reaction time and weaken attention and memory, and that the effects are strongest in the morning.

Sleep research points the same way. Well-known studies from the late 1990s and 2000 found that staying awake for around 17 to 19 hours impaired performance on attention and reaction tasks about as much as a BAC of roughly 0.05%, and longer periods awake were worse. A short, broken night after drinking puts you in that territory even before the hangover is counted.

### What a hangover does to the skills you need to drive

Driving uses a lot of mental resources at once. A hangover chips away at several of them:

- **Reaction time.** Slower reactions mean longer stopping distances. At highway speed, a fraction of a second covers a lot of road.
- **Sustained attention.** Long, boring stretches of road are exactly where hungover drivers struggle most, because staying focused takes effort you don't have.
- **Divided attention.** Checking mirrors, watching for pedestrians, and following directions at the same time gets harder.
- **Drowsiness and microsleeps.** Brief lapses of a few seconds can happen without you noticing them.
- **Headache, light sensitivity, and nausea.** These are distracting, and a sudden wave of nausea while driving is a real hazard.
- **Low blood sugar and dehydration.** Both can leave you shaky, foggy, and slower to think. Our [hangover symptoms guide](/never-hungover/hangover-symptoms) covers why these happen.

The tricky part is that you can feel fine sitting at the kitchen table and still be off when you're behind the wheel. Hangover impairment shows up most under load: in traffic, at night, on long drives, or when something unexpected happens.

## Can You Get a DUI the Day After Drinking?

Yes. A DUI is about your state when you are driving, not about when you drank. Morning-after DUIs are common enough that police in several countries run "morning after" awareness campaigns, especially around holidays.

Here's how the law generally works, with the caveat that rules vary by place and you should check your own local laws:

- **The standard US limit is 0.08% BAC** for adult drivers in non-commercial vehicles, in every state except Utah, which uses **0.05%**.
- **Commercial drivers** in the US are held to **0.04%**, and many employers and transport rules are stricter still.
- **Drivers under 21** face "zero tolerance" laws in every state, which usually means any measurable alcohol (often 0.02% or less) can lead to penalties.
- **You can be charged under the limit.** In the US, if an officer has reason to believe your driving is impaired by alcohol, you can be charged with impaired driving even with a BAC below 0.08%.
- **Outside the US, limits are often lower.** Many European countries use 0.05%, Scotland uses 0.05%, England and Wales use 0.08%, and some countries have limits at or near zero.

The practical point: if you had a heavy night and you're driving early, you are taking a legal risk as well as a safety one. Morning commutes, school runs, and early flights to catch are exactly when people get caught out.

### "But I feel fine"

How you feel is a poor measure of your BAC. As alcohol levels fall, the buzz fades well before the alcohol is gone, and the headache and fatigue of the hangover can mask how much is left. Many people who are stopped the morning after are genuinely surprised by their reading.

## Is There a Safe Time to Drive After Drinking?

People often want a number: "how many hours after drinking can I drive?" We're not going to give you one, because no honest number exists for your situation.

- **The "one drink per hour" figure is an average, not a promise.** Real clearance rates vary a lot with body size, sex, genetics, liver health, medicines, and how much you usually drink. You can't tell from the inside whether you're a fast or slow clearer today.
- **People count drinks badly.** Heavy pours, strong craft beers, doubles, and drinks topped up by someone else all make the night's total higher than it feels.
- **Zero alcohol isn't the finish line.** Even once your blood alcohol reaches zero, a hangover and a short night can still slow your reactions and attention, as the research above shows.
- **Feeling fine is the least reliable signal of all.** Impaired people are poor judges of their own impairment.

So the practical answer isn't a calculation. It's a decision made the night before: **if you're going to drink heavily, plan for the next morning to be car-free.** If that isn't possible, drink much less, or not at all.

### What doesn't sober you up faster

None of these lower your blood alcohol:

- **Coffee or energy drinks.** Caffeine can make you feel more alert, which may make you *more* confident than you should be. We explain why in our article on [mixing energy drinks and alcohol](/never-hungover/energy-drinks-and-alcohol).
- **A cold shower or fresh air.** They wake you up, but your liver works at the same speed.
- **A big breakfast.** Eating before or while drinking slows how fast alcohol gets into your blood. Eating the next morning doesn't speed up how fast it leaves.
- **Water and electrolytes.** These can help you feel less awful, but they don't flush alcohol out faster.
- **Exercise or sweating it out.** Only a tiny amount of alcohol leaves through sweat and breath. The liver does almost all the work.

Only time lowers your BAC.

## Should You Use a Breathalyzer Before Driving?

A personal breathalyzer can be a useful reality check, with some honest caveats:

- **It's best at telling you "no."** If it shows a meaningful reading the morning after, that's a strong signal to wait.
- **Accuracy varies a lot between devices.** Cheaper models can be off, and readings can be thrown off if you've recently used mouthwash, vomited, or just had a drink, because alcohol in the mouth gives a falsely high result. Wait at least 15 to 20 minutes after any of those before testing.
- **A low reading isn't a green light.** It says nothing about sleep loss, slow reactions, or a pounding headache. You can blow 0.00 and still be in no shape to drive on the highway.

Use it as one input, not as permission.

## Who Should Be Especially Careful

Some situations raise the stakes:

- **Commercial and professional drivers.** Lower legal limits, workplace testing, and much heavier consequences. Many employers have their own rules about drinking before shifts, and those often apply to the night before.
- **New and young drivers.** Less experience plus zero-tolerance rules is a bad mix with a hangover.
- **Anyone driving children or passengers.** Your risk becomes their risk.
- **Long drives and night drives.** Monotonous highway driving is where hangover-related drowsiness and lane drift show up most.
- **People taking medicines that cause drowsiness.** Many common products, including some sleep aids, older antihistamines like diphenhydramine, some cold and flu remedies, and many prescription drugs, cause drowsiness on their own and can add to leftover alcohol and fatigue. If a label says not to drive or operate machinery, take that seriously, and ask a pharmacist if you're unsure.
- **Pilots, boat operators, and people using heavy machinery.** Many of these have strict rules about hours between drinking and working, and often a lower alcohol limit than for car drivers.

## What to Do Instead of Driving Hungover

If there's any real doubt, the answer is to not drive yet. That's easier when you've planned ahead:

- **Decide the night before.** If you know you have to drive in the morning, set a cut-off time for your last drink and count backward from when you'll need to leave.
- **Plan the ride home *and* the ride back.** People often arrange a safe way home and forget they need their car the next morning. Leave it where it is and get a ride back to it later.
- **Use the alternatives.** Rideshare, a taxi, public transit, a friend who didn't drink, or simply rescheduling. A late start or a missed appointment is far cheaper than a crash or a DUI.
- **Give yourself the morning.** If you can, push driving to the afternoon. Each extra hour helps clear any remaining alcohol and lets the worst of the hangover pass.
- **Work from home or ask for flexibility.** If your job allows it, it's better to say you're running late than to risk the drive.

### Ways to make the morning after less rough

None of these make it safe to drive sooner, but they can make the day more bearable:

- **Drink water before bed and in the morning.** Alcohol makes you pee more and can leave you dehydrated.
- **Eat something with carbs and protein.** It can help with shakiness and low energy.
- **Rest.** Sleep debt is part of what makes a hangover feel so draining. If you can, take a nap before you need to be anywhere.
- **Go easy on painkillers.** If you take something for a headache, follow the label, eat first, and be careful with acetaminophen after heavy drinking. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains why.

For a fuller picture of how long the symptoms tend to last, see our guide to [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last).

## How to Avoid the Problem Next Time

The best way to avoid a hungover drive is to not end up in that spot. A few habits help:

- **Pace yourself.** Alternating alcoholic drinks with water slows you down and cuts the total.
- **Eat before and while you drink.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood and tends to lower your peak BAC.
- **Stop earlier.** Every hour between your last drink and your drive is an hour of clearing time.
- **Count standard drinks, not glasses.** Big pours and strong beers add up fast.
- **Make driving plans before you start drinking,** not at midnight when your judgment is already affected.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes into more depth on the habits that actually make a difference.

### Where DHM fits, and where it doesn't

Dihydromyricetin (DHM) is a plant compound that some people take around drinking to ease how they feel the next day. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data so far, so it's promising rather than settled. It's important to be clear about one thing: **there is no good evidence that DHM lowers your blood alcohol or makes it safe to drive sooner.** It won't change your breathalyzer reading or the law, and it doesn't replace waiting.

If you'd like to try it for hangover symptoms on a night when you're not driving anywhere, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

Driving hungover is legal only if you're under the limit, and the morning after a heavy night, you may not be. Your body clears roughly one drink per hour, nothing speeds it up, and sleep doesn't reset the clock. Even when the alcohol is gone, a hangover and a short night can leave you slower and less alert in ways research has compared to mild intoxication. If you drank a lot, finished late, or feel foggy, don't drive: get a ride or take transit, and next time plan a car-free morning before the night starts. When it comes to driving, "probably fine" isn't good enough.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drive hungover?**

Legally, you can drive if your blood alcohol is under the limit, but that doesn't mean you're safe. Simulator research suggests a hangover alone, with no alcohol left in the blood, can make driving worse in ways similar to a mild level of intoxication. And many people who feel hungover still have alcohol in their system. If you drank heavily, don't drive: get a ride or take transit.

**Can you get a DUI the morning after drinking?**

Yes. A DUI depends on your blood alcohol and your impairment when you're driving, not on when you had your last drink. If you went to bed late after heavy drinking, you can still be at or over the limit the next morning. In the US you can also be charged below 0.08% if an officer believes you're impaired, and limits are lower for commercial drivers, for drivers under 21, and in Utah (0.05%).

**How long after drinking is it safe to drive?**

There's no safe number of hours that applies to you personally. The often-quoted figure of about one standard drink cleared per hour is only an average, and real rates vary widely. After a heavy night you can still have alcohol in your blood the next morning, and even after it's gone, hangover symptoms and lost sleep can slow you down. If you're drinking heavily, plan a car-free next morning instead of trying to calculate when you'll be fine.

**Is driving hungover as bad as driving drunk?**

Not exactly the same, but it can be closer than people think. A 2014 driving-simulator study from Utrecht University found that hungover drivers with zero alcohol in their blood weaved within their lane more than when they weren't hungover, by an amount the researchers compared to driving with a blood alcohol level of around 0.05%. That is a single lab study, but it fits with what we know about sleep loss and fatigue.

**Does coffee or a cold shower sober you up enough to drive?**

No. Coffee, cold showers, food, exercise, and water don't speed up how fast your liver clears alcohol. Caffeine can make you feel more alert, which can make it easier to misjudge how impaired you are. Only time lowers your blood alcohol.

**Can I use a personal breathalyzer to decide if I can drive?**

It can tell you that you're clearly not ready, but a low reading isn't a green light. Consumer devices vary in accuracy, and a reading under the limit says nothing about the fatigue and slow reactions a hangover brings. If the device shows any alcohol after a heavy night, treat that as a reason to wait.

**Does DHM help you drive sooner after drinking?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM lowers blood alcohol in people or makes it safe to drive sooner. Some people take it for hangover symptoms, but it should never factor into a decision about getting behind the wheel.
